"... when the winds blow for their neighbours..."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 50, verses 16–21:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.﴾ ﴿When the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left.﴾ ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer, ready.﴾ ﴿And the stupor of death will come with truth. That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾ ﴿And the Horn will be blown. That is the Day of the Threat.﴾ ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾

These are verses in which proofs are established against the disbelievers in their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense. "Al-khalq" (creation) is bringing a thing into being according to a measure and an arrangement in a judgmental sense. "Al-insan" is a generic noun (ism al-jins). Some commentators said that "al-insan" here refers to Adam, peace be upon him. "Tuwaswisu" means: it speaks within its thought. The sound of jewelry is called "waswasa" because of its faintness, and "waswasa" is only used for what is not good.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ is an expression for God's power over the servant. The servant being within the grip of power and knowledge, and being encompassed by it, so the nearness is by power and authority, since nothing hidden or manifest is concealed from the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted. Every physical thing that is near has a barrier between it and the heart of a human being. "Al-warid" is a large vein in the neck. It is said that there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. Al-Farra' said: it is what lies between the windpipe and the two collarbones (al-'ilbawayn). Al-Hasan said: "al-warid" is "al-wataan" (the aorta). Al-Ashram said: it is the river of the body. In the heart it is the wataan, in the back the abhar, and in the arm and thigh the akhal and the nasa, and in the little finger the usaylim. "Al-habl" (rope/vein) is a shared term (ism mushtarak), so its specification is by its annexation to "al-warid." This is not the annexation of a thing to itself, but like the annexation of a genus to its species, as you say: "the living of the bird is not permitted with its meat."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾, the commentators said: the governing element of "idh" (when) is "aqrab" (closer). It is possible in my view that its governing element is a hidden verb whose estimate is: "Remember when they receive." This meaning is fitting, because He informed of the creation as a bare report, and of the knowledge of the thoughts of souls, and of the nearness by power and dominion. When the report was complete, He informed with the mention of circumstances that confirm this report and show its arrival to the hearer. Among them: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾; among them the coming of the stupor of death; among them the blowing of the Horn; and among them the coming of every soul. "Al-mutalaqqiyan" are the two angels entrusted with every person: the angel of the right who writes the good deeds, and the angel of the left who writes the bad deeds. Al-Hasan said: the guardians are four, two by day and two by night.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is supported by the hadith: "Angels succeed one another among you, angels by night and angels by day..." the hadith in its entirety. It is also narrated that the angel of the right is a leader over the angel of the left, and that when the servant commits a sin, the angel of the right says to the other: "Hold off, perhaps he will repent." This was narrated by Ibrahim al-Taymi and Sufyan al-Thawri.

"Qa'id" (seated) means: sitting. Some said it is in the sense of "akil" (eating), so it means "maq'id" (place of sitting). The Kufans said: he intended "qu'udan" (sitting), so the singular was placed in the position of the plural genus. The first view is more correct, because the sitting-places (maqa'id) are only at the sitting of a person, whereas "qa'id" can be said of a person in every state. Mujahid said: "qa'id" means "rasad" (a watcher). The view of Sibawayh is that the estimate is: "on the right, a seated one; and on the left, a seated one," so the mention of the second was sufficient instead of the first. Similar to this, in his view, is the verse:

"...and the stubbornness of one who procrastinates, whose creditor is worn out"

And similar is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed I guaranteed to whoever came to me what he committed, and my father did, and I was not treacherous."

Such examples are numerous. The view of al-Mubarrad is that the estimate is: "on the right, a seated one; and on the left," and the word "qa'id" is moved from its place. The view of al-Farra' is that the word "qa'id" indicates the dual and the plural, so it needs no estimate beyond what is apparent.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He does not utter a word﴾, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatada said: the two angels write the speech, and Allah confirms from it the good deeds and the bad deeds and erases what is other than that. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Abu al-Jawza' and Mujahid said: they write down everything for him, even his groaning during his illness. Ikrima said: the meaning is: he does not utter any word, good or bad; as for what goes beyond this, it is not written. The first view is more correct. It is narrated that a man said to his camel, "Halla!" (a command to make it kneel). The angel of the right said: "I will not write it." The angel of the left said: "I will not write it." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed to the angel of the left: "Write what the angel of the right has left out." A similar report is narrated from Hisham al-Himsi. This word, if considered, depends on the intention of its speaker concerning his camel. If he was in obedience, then "halla" is a good deed; if he was in disobedience, then it is a bad deed. What lies between these two is rare to find, and there must be accompanying circumstances for every state of a person that make it purely for good or for its opposite. Al-Tha'labi related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The seat of the two angels is on the two front teeth; their pen is the tongue and their ink is the saliva." Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: their seat is beneath the hair. Al-Hasan used to like to clean his goatee for this reason. Al-Hasan said: when a person dies, his record is folded up, and it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Read your book; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra: 14]. By Allah, he was just who made himself his own reckoner.

"Raqib" means the observer, and "'atid" means the present, ready.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "wa jaat" (and it came): in my view it is coordinated (ataf) to His saying, the Exalted: "idh yatalaqqa" (when he receives). The estimate is: "and when the stupor of death comes." He placed the past tense in the position of the future to confirm and establish the matter, and this is more urgent for preparation and for feeling the nearness. This is the way of the Arabs in that. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ and ﴿And every soul will come﴾, for these are a transformation that carries the sense of the future. Abu 'Amr recited ﴿wa jaat sakratu﴾ with the assimilation of the taa' into the seen. ﴿Indeed, We created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.﴾ ﴿When the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left.﴾ ﴿He does not utter a word except that with him is an observer, ready.﴾ ﴿And the stupor of death will come with truth. That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾ ﴿And the Horn will be blown. That is the Day of the Threat.﴾ ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.﴾

These are verses in which proofs are established against the disbelievers in their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense. "Al-khalq" (creation) is bringing a thing into being according to a measure and an arrangement in a judgmental sense. "Al-insan" is a generic noun (ism al-jins). Some commentators said that "al-insan" here refers to Adam, peace be upon him. "Tuwaswisu" means: it speaks within its thought. The sound of jewelry is called "waswasa" because of its faintness, and "waswasa" is only used for what is not good.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ is an expression for God's power over the servant. The servant being within the grip of power and knowledge, and being encompassed by it, so the nearness is by power and authority, since nothing hidden or manifest is concealed from the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted. Every physical thing that is near has a barrier between it and the heart of a human being. "Al-warid" is a large vein in the neck. It is said that there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. Al-Farra' said: it is what lies between the windpipe and the two collarbones (al-'ilbawayn). Al-Hasan said: "al-warid" is "al-wataan" (the aorta). Al-Ashram said: it is the river of the body. In the heart it is the wataan, in the back the abhar, and in the arm and thigh the akhal and the nasa, and in the little finger the usaylim. "Al-habl" (rope/vein) is a shared term (ism mushtarak), so its specification is by its annexation to "al-warid." This is not the annexation of a thing to itself, but like the annexation of a genus to its species, as you say: "the living of the bird is not permitted with its meat."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾, the commentators said: the governing element of "idh" (when) is "aqrab" (closer). It is possible in my view that its governing element is a hidden verb whose estimate is: "Remember when they receive." This meaning is fitting, because He informed of the creation as a bare report, and of the knowledge of the thoughts of souls, and of the nearness by power and dominion. When the report was complete, He informed with the mention of circumstances that confirm this report and show its arrival to the hearer. Among them: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾; among them the coming of the stupor of death; among them the blowing of the Horn; and among them the coming of every soul. "Al-mutalaqqiyan" are the two angels entrusted with every person: the angel of the right who writes the good deeds, and the angel of the left who writes the bad deeds. Al-Hasan said: the guardians are four, two by day and two by night.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is supported by the hadith: "Angels succeed one another among you, angels by night and angels by day..." the hadith in its entirety. It is also narrated that the angel of the right is a leader over the angel of the left, and that when the servant commits a sin, the angel of the right says to the other: "Hold off, perhaps he will repent." This was narrated by Ibrahim al-Taymi and Sufyan al-Thawri.

"Qa'id" (seated) means: sitting. Some said it is in the sense of "akil" (eating), so it means "maq'id" (place of sitting). The Kufans said: he intended "qu'udan" (sitting), so the singular was placed in the position of the plural genus. The first view is more correct, because the sitting-places (maqa'id) are only at the sitting of a person, whereas "qa'id" can be said of a person in every state. Mujahid said: "qa'id" means "rasad" (a watcher). The view of Sibawayh is that the estimate is: "on the right, a seated one; and on the left, a seated one," so the mention of the second was sufficient instead of the first. Similar to this, in his view, is the verse:

"...and the stubbornness of one who procrastinates, whose creditor is worn out"

And similar is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed I guaranteed to whoever came to me what he committed, and my father did, and I was not treacherous."

Such examples are numerous. The view of al-Mubarrad is that the estimate is: "on the right, a seated one; and on the left," and the word "qa'id" is moved from its place. The view of al-Farra' is that the word "qa'id" indicates the dual and the plural, so it needs no estimate beyond what is apparent.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He does not utter a word﴾, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatada said: the two angels write the speech, and Allah confirms from it the good deeds and the bad deeds and erases what is other than that. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Abu al-Jawza' and Mujahid said: they write down everything for him, even his groaning during his illness. Ikrima said: the meaning is: he does not utter any word, good or bad; as for what goes beyond this, it is not written. The first view is more correct. It is narrated that a man said to his camel, "Halla!" (a command to make it kneel). The angel of the right said: "I will not write it." The angel of the left said: "I will not write it." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed to the angel of the left: "Write what the angel of the right has left out." A similar report is narrated from Hisham al-Himsi. This word, if considered, depends on the intention of its speaker concerning his camel. If he was in obedience, then "halla" is a good deed; if he was in disobedience, then it is a bad deed. What lies between these two is rare to find, and there must be accompanying circumstances for every state of a person that make it purely for good or for its opposite. Al-Tha'labi related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The seat of the two angels is on the two front teeth; their pen is the tongue and their ink is the saliva." Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: their seat is beneath the hair. Al-Hasan used to like to clean his goatee for this reason. Al-Hasan said: when a person dies, his record is folded up, and it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Read your book; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra: 14]. By Allah, he was just who made himself his own reckoner.

"Raqib" means the observer, and "'atid" means the present, ready.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "wa jaat" (and it came): in my view it is coordinated (ataf) to His saying, the Exalted: "idh yatalaqqa" (when he receives). The estimate is: "and when the stupor of death comes." He placed the past tense in the position of the future to confirm and establish the matter, and this is more urgent for preparation and for feeling the nearness. This is the way of the Arabs in that. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ and ﴿And every soul will come﴾, for these are a transformation that carries the sense of the future. Abu 'Amr recited ﴿wa jaat sakratu﴾ with the assimilation of the taa' into the seen. The stupor of death (sakrat al-mawt) is what afflicts a person at the time of his death-agony, and people differ in their states within it, but each person has a stupor. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say, regarding "Indeed for death there are agonies" (inna lil-mawti lasakarat).

His saying, the Exalted: "bi-l-haqq" (with truth) means: with the meeting with Allah, blessed and exalted, and the loss of the worldly life. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "wa jaat sakratu al-haqqi bi-l-mawt" (the stupor of the truth came with death). Ibn Jubayr and Talha recited it this way. It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said it to his daughter Aisha, may Allah be pleased with them both, because she sat at his head weeping while he was in his death-agony. She said:

"By your life, wealth does not avail a youth when on a day the breath rattles and the chest is constricted."

Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, opened his eyes and said: "Do not say it like this, but say: ﴿And the stupor of the truth came with death; that is what you were trying to avoid﴾." This hadith was related on the authority of the well-known reciters with the reading ﴿and the stupor of death came with truth﴾. Abu al-Fath said: if you wish, you attach the "ba'" (with) to "jaat" as you say, "I brought Zayd" (ji'tu bi-Zayd), meaning: I drove him. And if you wish, it is by an estimate: "and with it is death."

The interpreters differed on the meaning of ﴿and the stupor of the truth came with death﴾. Al-Tabari said, and al-Tha'labi related it: "al-haqq" is Allah, the Exalted. In annexing the stupor to the name of Allah, the Exalted, there is a remoteness, although it is permissible from the standpoint that it is a creation of His; but the eloquence of the Qur'an and its arrangement do not admit this. Some interpreters said: the meaning is: "and the stupor of parting from life came with death," and parting from life is a truth that a person knows, and he turns away from it with his hope. The meaning of this turning away is that he says: "I will live such and such," so whenever he thinks of the nearness of death, he turns his mind and hope to a far distance in time. Also, a person's caution, his precautions, and the like are all turning away.

The blowing of the Horn has been discussed many times before, and "the Day of the Threat" is the Day of Resurrection, and He annexed it to "the Threat" to frighten.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾. Talha ibn Musarrif recited "mahha" with a heavy ha'. "Al-sa'iq" is the one urging to march. People differed about the driver and the witness. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Mujahid, and others said: they are two angels entrusted with each person, one of whom drives him and the other, from among his guardians, bears witness against him. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the deed. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the Prophet ﷺ. He said: it was also said: the witness is the book that he meets, opened. Some of the theorists said: "sa'iq" is a generic noun, and "shahid" likewise. So the drivers of people are angels who are entrusted with that, and the witnesses are the guardians in this world and everything that bears witness. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the limbs of the human being. This is remote for Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because the limbs only bear witness to disobedience. His saying, the Exalted: "kullu nafs" (every soul) includes the righteous, so its meaning is: and a witness to his good and his evil. In "shahid" the generic sense is stronger, so the angels and the places bear witness to the good, and from this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No one hears the reach of the caller's voice (muadhdhin), neither human nor jinn nor anything, except that it will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection." Likewise the angels, the places, and the limbs bear witness to the evil.

Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the driver is an angel and the witness is the deed. Ibn Muslim said: the driver is a devil. Al-Tha'labi related this from him. The view in the book of Mundhir ibn Sa'id is weak.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He does not utter a word﴾, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatada said: the two angels write the speech, and Allah confirms from it the good deeds and the bad deeds and erases what is other than that. This is the apparent meaning of the verse. Abu al-Jawza' and Mujahid said: they write down everything for him, even his groaning during his illness. Ikrima said: the meaning is: he does not utter any word, good or bad; as for what goes beyond this, it is not written. The first view is more correct. It is narrated that a man said to his camel, "Halla!" (a command to make it kneel). The angel of the right said: "I will not write it." The angel of the left said: "I will not write it." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed to the angel of the left: "Write what the angel of the right has left out." A similar report is narrated from Hisham al-Himsi. This word, if considered, depends on the intention of its speaker concerning his camel. If he was in obedience, then "halla" is a good deed; if he was in disobedience, then it is a bad deed. What lies between these two is rare to find, and there must be accompanying circumstances for every state of a person that make it purely for good or for its opposite. Al-Tha'labi related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "The seat of the two angels is on the two front teeth; their pen is the tongue and their ink is the saliva." Al-Dahhak and al-Hasan said: their seat is beneath the hair. Al-Hasan used to like to clean his goatee for this reason. Al-Hasan said: when a person dies, his record is folded up, and it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Read your book; sufficient is yourself today as a reckoner against you﴾ [al-Isra: 14]. By Allah, he was just who made himself his own reckoner.

"Raqib" means the observer, and "'atid" means the present, ready.

As for His saying, the Exalted: "wa jaat" (and it came): in my view it is coordinated (ataf) to His saying, the Exalted: "idh yatalaqqa" (when he receives). The estimate is: "and when the stupor of death comes." He placed the past tense in the position of the future to confirm and establish the matter, and this is more urgent for preparation and for feeling the nearness. This is the way of the Arabs in that. This is clarified by His saying: ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ and ﴿And every soul will come﴾, for these are a transformation that carries the sense of the future. Abu 'Amr recited ﴿wa jaat sakratu﴾ with the assimilation of the taa' into the seen. The stupor of death (sakrat al-mawt) is what afflicts a person at the time of his death-agony, and people differ in their states within it, but each person has a stupor. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say, regarding "Indeed for death there are agonies" (inna lil-mawti lasakarat).

His saying, the Exalted: "bi-l-haqq" (with truth) means: with the meeting with Allah, blessed and exalted, and the loss of the worldly life. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "wa jaat sakratu al-haqqi bi-l-mawt" (the stupor of the truth came with death). Ibn Jubayr and Talha recited it this way. It is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said it to his daughter Aisha, may Allah be pleased with them both, because she sat at his head weeping while he was in his death-agony. She said:

"By your life, wealth does not avail a youth when on a day the breath rattles and the chest is constricted."

Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, opened his eyes and said: "Do not say it like this, but say: ﴿And the stupor of the truth came with death; that is what you were trying to avoid﴾." This hadith was related on the authority of the well-known reciters with the reading ﴿and the stupor of death came with truth﴾. Abu al-Fath said: if you wish, you attach the "ba'" (with) to "jaat" as you say, "I brought Zayd" (ji'tu bi-Zayd), meaning: I drove him. And if you wish, it is by an estimate: "and with it is death."

The interpreters differed on the meaning of ﴿and the stupor of the truth came with death﴾. Al-Tabari said, and al-Tha'labi related it: "al-haqq" is Allah, the Exalted. In annexing the stupor to the name of Allah, the Exalted, there is a remoteness, although it is permissible from the standpoint that it is a creation of His; but the eloquence of the Qur'an and its arrangement do not admit this. Some interpreters said: the meaning is: "and the stupor of parting from life came with death," and parting from life is a truth that a person knows, and he turns away from it with his hope. The meaning of this turning away is that he says: "I will live such and such," so whenever he thinks of the nearness of death, he turns his mind and hope to a far distance in time. Also, a person's caution, his precautions, and the like are all turning away.

The blowing of the Horn has been discussed many times before, and "the Day of the Threat" is the Day of Resurrection, and He annexed it to "the Threat" to frighten.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾. Talha ibn Musarrif recited "mahha" with a heavy ha'. "Al-sa'iq" is the one urging to march. People differed about the driver and the witness. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Mujahid, and others said: they are two angels entrusted with each person, one of whom drives him and the other, from among his guardians, bears witness against him. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the deed. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the Prophet ﷺ. He said: it was also said: the witness is the book that he meets, opened. Some of the theorists said: "sa'iq" is a generic noun, and "shahid" likewise. So the drivers of people are angels who are entrusted with that, and the witnesses are the guardians in this world and everything that bears witness. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the driver is an angel, and the witness is the limbs of the human being. This is remote for Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because the limbs only bear witness to disobedience. His saying, the Exalted: "kullu nafs" (every soul) includes the righteous, so its meaning is: and a witness to his good and his evil. In "shahid" the generic sense is stronger, so the angels and the places bear witness to the good, and from this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "No one hears the reach of the caller's voice (muadhdhin), neither human nor jinn nor anything, except that it will testify for him on the Day of Resurrection." Likewise the angels, the places, and the limbs bear witness to the evil.

Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the driver is an angel and the witness is the deed. Ibn Muslim said: the driver is a devil. Al-Tha'labi related this from him. The view in the book of Mundhir ibn Sa'id is weak.

(p-45) God, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿You were heedless of this, so We removed your covering, and today your sight is piercing.﴾ ﴿His companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ ﴿"Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever,﴾ ﴿who forbids good, transgresses, and is in doubt,﴾ ﴿who set up another god alongside God. Cast him into the severe punishment."﴾ ﴿His companion will say, "Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious, but he was in far-off error."﴾ ﴿He will say, "Do not dispute in My presence, for I had already sent forward to you the warning."﴾

Al-Jahdari recited, "لَقَدْ كُنْتِ" (laqad kunti) with a kasra on the ta', addressing the soul (nafs), and likewise the kasras on the following kafs. Salih ibn Kaysan, al-Dahhak and Ibn 'Abbas said that the meaning of God's words "You were indeed (heedless)" is that it is said to the heedless disbeliever, among those with whom there is a driver and a witness, when he stands before the Most Merciful, Mighty and Majestic, and witnesses the realities that he did not believe in during the world and used to ignore and not consider: "You were heedless of this. Now that the covering has been removed from you, your sight is sharp," meaning your insight is keen. This is like saying, "So-and-so is sharp of mind and heart," and the like. Mujahid said it refers to the sight of the eye, meaning that his gaze became intense toward his scale and the other terrors of the Resurrection. Zayd ibn Aslam said: God's words, "You were indeed (heedless)," are addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning is that he was addressed with this in the world, that is: "You were indeed, O Muhammad, heedless of knowing this narrative and the unseen until We sent you, bestowed favour upon you and taught you, so your sight today is sharp."

This interpretation is weak for several reasons. The first is that heedlessness (ghafla) is always attributed to one who falls short, and Muhammad (ﷺ) had no shortcoming before his mission or after it. The second is that God's words after this, "His companion will say," require that the pronoun refer to the nearest preceding mention. The one who is told, "Your sight today is sharp," if we take it as referring to the one with the soul in the previous verse, then this objection comes between the two speeches to Muhammad (ﷺ) without being properly connected, so consider this. The third is that the meaning of rebuking and reproaching the disbeliever for his condition in the world falls away, and that is more fitting for the verse and better suited to its arrangement. In my view, the correct position is what al-Hasan and Salim ibn 'Abd Allah said, that it is addressed to the human being with the soul mentioned, whether believer or disbeliever.

As for ﴿We removed your covering﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: it is life after death.

As for God's words, ﴿His companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾, a group of exegetes (mufassirun) said: his companion is one of the guardians (zabaniyya) of Hell, meaning he said: this punishment that is for this disbelieving human being is present and ready.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this there is an incitement against the disbeliever and a hastening of his punishment.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: rather, his companion is the angel assigned to drive him. It is as if he said: this disbeliever who was assigned to be driven is present with me. Al-Zahrawi said: "His companion" is his devil (shaytan). This is weak. What led to it is that the companion in God's words, "Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious," is undisputedly his devil in the world who misled him. The word qarin is a generic noun (ism jins), so his driver is a companion, his companion from among the guardians is a companion, and the recorder of his evil deeds in the world is a companion, and this verse may include all of them, meaning: this one whom I have counted against him is ready with Me and entails his punishment. One who walks alongside a person on his path is a companion. The poet said:

"Do not ask about a man; ask about his companion, for every companion follows his companion."

The companion in this verse is different from the companion in God's words, "His companion will say, 'Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious,'" since companionship takes various forms. Some scholars said: his companion in this verse is his deed, of heart and limbs.

As for God's words, ﴿Cast into Hell﴾, their meaning is: it is said, "Cast into Hell." People differed about to whom this is said. A group of exegetes said it is a statement to two angels of the angels of punishment. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, in the book of al-Zahrawi, said it is a statement to the driver and the witness. Al-Zahrawi related that the one commanded to cast the disbeliever into the Fire is two. On these two views, there is no consideration of God's words, "Cast." Mujahid and a group of those who interpret said it is a statement to the companion, either the driver or the one who is among the guardians, as previously stated. The proponents of this view differed about the meaning of God's words, "Cast," when it is addressed to one. Al-Mubarrad said: its meaning is "Cast, cast," for he intended the repetition of the command for emphasis and affirmation. He returned the dual to the pronoun for brevity, as the poet said:

"... he seized you with two (lashes) upon a bowman."

He means: "Shoot, shoot." Some of those who interpret said the intended form is "alqayn," and the nun was replaced by an alif, just as the alif replaces tanwin. A group of people of knowledge in the language of the Arabs said: this follows the custom of the Arabs, because it was common among them that three would travel together on journeys and the like, so each of them addresses two. This became frequent in their speech and poetry until it became a convention in address, and it was then used for one person. From this comes their saying in poetry: "My friend," "my companion," "stop, let us weep," and the like. The narrators have followed this practice, so one says, "He narrated to us," even if he heard it alone. A parallel to this verse in this matter is al-Zajjaj's saying: "O my two guards, strike his neck," and this is evidence of the Arab custom. From it is the poet's saying:

"If you two restrain me by (invoking) the son of Affan, I will be restrained; and if you two leave me, I will defend a protected honour."

(p-47) Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "ألْقِيًا" with tanwin on "ألْقِيا." "Kaffar" is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha). "Anid" means one who opposes the truth, that is, one who deviates from it.

God's words, ﴿who forbids good﴾, is a general term covering wealth, good speech, and cooperation in matters. Qatada, Mujahid and Ikrima said its meaning is the obligatory zakat. This specification is weak. ﴿Transgresses﴾ means with his tongue and his hand. ﴿In doubt﴾ means engaged in what causes doubt, from "araba al-rajul" when a man commits a dubious act and enters into it. Al-Tha'labi said: it was said that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Al-Hasan said: "in doubt" means one who is skeptical about God, Most High, and His religion.

God's words, ﴿who set up another god alongside God﴾, the verse may be such that "who" is a substitute (badal) for "disbeliever," and it may be a qualifier of it, since "disbeliever" is specified by the described attributes mentioned, so it is permissible to describe it with this definite term. It may also be that "who" is the subject (mubtada') and its predicate is God's words, ﴿cast him﴾, and the fa' entered for the ambiguity contained in "who," so there arose a resemblance to the conditional. There is consideration in this. It seems to me most likely that "who" is the subject, and the speech then includes the children of Adam and the devils who misled them in the world. For this reason the companion, the misleading devil of the world, was stirred and sought to clear himself and exonerate himself by saying to his Lord, (p-48) ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious﴾. His statement, ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious﴾, is not a valid argument, because it is a lie in denying that he led him astray, while the reality is that he led him astray through whispering and adornment. God, Most High, also led him astray by creating and originating, according to His prior decree, which is justice from Him, with no lord besides Him. He is described as being in "far-off error" by way of hyperbole, meaning that his return to guidance is impossible.

God's words, ﴿Do not dispute﴾, mean: God, Most High, said, "Do not dispute in My presence with this kind of talk, which benefits nothing, since all of you have deserved the Fire." God, Most High, has informed us that disputes take place before Him concerning wrongs and the like, in which there is retaliation and claiming of rights. God, Most High, confirmed this with His words, ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute﴾ [al-Zumar: 31]. The plural pronoun in God's words, "Do not dispute," is intended by God to address all the companions, since it is a general command that is not restricted to two only. This is like a judge saying to two litigants, "Do not be harsh with me," intending the two litigants and whoever is in their position. ﴿I had already sent forward to you the warning﴾ means what the messengers, peace be upon them, and the books brought concerning the punishment of the disbelievers.

"... he seized you with two (lashes) upon a bowman."

He means: "Shoot, shoot." Some of those who interpret said the intended form is "alqayn," and the nun was replaced by an alif, just as the alif replaces tanwin. "If you two restrain me by (invoking) the son of Affan, I will be restrained; and if you two leave me, I will defend a protected honour."

Al-Tha'labi said: it was said that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Al-Hasan said: "in doubt" means one who is skeptical about God, Most High, and His religion.

God, Most High, also led him astray by creating and originating, according to His prior decree, which is justice from Him, with no lord besides Him. He is described as being in "far-off error" by way of hyperbole, meaning that his return to guidance is impossible.

Al-Jahdari recited, "لَقَدْ كُنْتِ" (laqad kunti) with a kasra on the ta', addressing the soul (nafs), and likewise the kasras on the following kafs. Now that the covering has been removed from you, your sight is sharp," meaning your insight is keen. This is like saying, "So-and-so is sharp of mind and heart," and the like. Mujahid said it refers to the sight of the eye, meaning that his gaze became intense toward his scale and the other terrors of the Resurrection. Zayd ibn Aslam said: God's words, "You were indeed (heedless)," are addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and the meaning is that he was addressed with this in the world, that is: "You were indeed, O Muhammad, heedless of knowing this narrative and the unseen until We sent you, bestowed favour upon you and taught you, so your sight today is sharp."

This interpretation is weak for several reasons. The first is that heedlessness (ghafla) is always attributed to one who falls short, and Muhammad (ﷺ) had no shortcoming before his mission or after it. The second is that God's words after this, "His companion will say," require that the pronoun refer to the nearest preceding mention. The one who is told, "Your sight today is sharp," if we take it as referring to the one with the soul in the previous verse, then this objection comes between the two speeches to Muhammad (ﷺ) without being properly connected, so consider this. The third is that the meaning of rebuking and reproaching the disbeliever for his condition in the world falls away, and that is more fitting for the verse and better suited to its arrangement. In my view, the correct position is what al-Hasan and Salim ibn 'Abd Allah said, that it is addressed to the human being with the soul mentioned, whether believer or disbeliever.

As for ﴿We removed your covering﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: it is life after death.

As for God's words, ﴿His companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾, a group of exegetes (mufassirun) said: his companion is one of the guardians (zabaniyya) of Hell, meaning he said: this punishment that is for this disbelieving human being is present and ready.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this there is an incitement against the disbeliever and a hastening of his punishment.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: rather, his companion is the angel assigned to drive him. It is as if he said: this disbeliever who was assigned to be driven is present with me. What led to it is that the companion in God's words, "Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious," is undisputedly his devil in the world who misled him. One who walks alongside a person on his path is a companion. The poet said:

"Do not ask about a man; ask about his companion, for every companion follows his companion."

The companion in this verse is different from the companion in God's words, "His companion will say, 'Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious,'" since companionship takes various forms. Some scholars said: his companion in this verse is his deed, of heart and limbs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 50, verses 29–35:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿The Word is not changed with Me, nor am I unjust to the servants.﴾ ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ ﴿And Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, not far off.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised, for every returner (awwab), keeper (hafiz).﴾ ﴿Whoever feared the All-Merciful in the unseen and came with a contrite heart.﴾ ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity.﴾ ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more.﴾

The meaning: He has already presented the threat that He will punish the disbelievers in His Fire, so "the Word is not changed with Me," and what My speech has decreed is not diminished. Then He removed the place of objection by His saying, "nor am I unjust to the servants," meaning: this is justice toward them, because I have given warning, granted respite, bestowed faculties of perception, guided them to the path and the two highways, and sent the Messengers. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of His saying, "The Word is not changed with Me," is that it is not falsified before Me, since I have knowledge of all matters; so the reference, according to this, is to the falsehood of the one who said, "I did not make him transgress." His saying, "On the Day We say to Hell," may have as its governing element His saying "nor am I unjust to the servants," and it may be governed by a hidden verb. The majority of reciters, and Hafs from 'Asim, read "naqulu" with the nun, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash, and Abu 'Ali preferred it on account of what preceded: His saying "I have sent forward" and His saying "nor am I." Nafi' and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "yaqulu" (He says), meaning Allah says; this is the reading of al-A'raj, Shayba, and the people of Madina. al-Hasan, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-A'mash also read "yuqalu" (it is said) in the passive form.

His saying "Are you filled?" is a questioning for affirmation and confirmation. People differed as to whether this affirmation occurred so that it was filled, or whether it was not filled. Those who held that it was filled, by every opinion of a group of interpreters, interpreted accordingly her saying "Is there any more?" Whoever said that it was filled took her saying, "Is there any more?" to mean a confirmation and negation of more, i.e., "Is there in My presence a place where anything can be added?" A similar interpretation is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And has 'Aqil left us any dwelling?" This is the interpretation of al-Hasan, 'Amr, and Wasil. Whoever said that it was not full took her saying, "Is there any more?" to mean a question and a desire for increase. al-Rummani said: it was said that the meaning is that its guardians say it; but that it is the one speaking is more apparent.

People differed regarding Hell's saying: is it literal or figurative? That is, its state is that of one who, if it spoke, would say such and such; this is like the line:

"My camel complained to me of the length of the journey,"

and like the line of Dhu al-Rummah:

"... its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

What is preferred regarding Hell's saying, "Is there any more?", is that it is literal, that it said this while not yet full, and this is the saying of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him. A sound, widely transmitted hadith clarifies this, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah says to Hell: Are you filled? It says: Is there any more? until the Mighty One places His foot in it, and it says: Enough, enough, and parts of it draw together with others." People have been at variance regarding the meaning of this hadith. A group of theologians held that "al-Jabbar" (the Mighty One) is a generic noun, and that it refers to the tyrants among the children of Adam. It is narrated that Allah counts among the tyrants a group whom He fills Hell with at the end. It is also narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that the skin of the disbeliever will become forty cubits thick, and his body will grow large in proportion to this; all of this is part of filling Hell. The majority held that al-Jabbar is a name of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and this is the correct view, for in the sound hadith: "So the Lord of the worlds places His foot in it." The interpretation of this is that "qadam" (foot) is what He has sent forward for it from His creation, whom He placed in His knowledge as its inhabitants. From this is His saying: ﴿And give good news to those who believed that they have a sure footing (qadam sidq) with their Lord﴾ [Yunus: 2]. So "qadam" is whatever has been sent forward of a thing. From this is the poet's saying:

"Connect yourself to your Lord and take for yourself a foot (qadam) that will save you on the Day of stumbling and slipping."

From this is al-'Ajjaj's saying:

"... and He establishes kingship for a king of foot (dhi qadam)."

That is, of advanced nobility. This interpretation is narrated from Ibn al-Mubarak and from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, and it is the saying of the scholars of usul. In the book of Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj: "So the Mighty One places His leg in it." Its meaning is the gathering which He has prepared for it; the term "rijl" (leg) is used for a large number of people, by likening them to a locust's leg. The poet said:

"A leg of people passed by it, and there withdrew towards them from the Yemeni tribe a crowd of men."

The criterion for consideration in this hadith is that bodily organ, likeness, and what is similar to them are all negated; nothing remains but the bringing out of expressions in these permissible ways in the speech of the Arabs.

"Uzlifat" means: was brought near. His saying, "not far off," is emphasis and clarification that this nearness is in distance, because "brought near" might have been understood as meaning by promise and information; the possibility was removed by His saying "not far off."

His saying, "This is what you were promised," is the verse. It may mean: it will be said to them in the Hereafter when Paradise is brought near, "This is what you were promised in the world." It may also mean an address to the community of Muhammad ﷺ, i.e., "This is what you, O people, are promised, for every returner (awwab) and keeper (hafiz)." "Awwab" is one who returns to obedience and to the right guidance of his soul. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: the awwab is the one who glorifies (musabbih), from His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10]. al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: he is the one who remembers his sins and seeks forgiveness. al-Muhasibi said: he is the one whose heart turns to Allah, the Exalted. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: we used to say that he is the one who, when he rises from his gathering, seeks Allah's forgiveness for what took place in that gathering, and the Prophet ﷺ used to do likewise. "Hafiz" means: keeping Allah's commands, so that he complies with them, and abandoning His prohibitions. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he is one who guards his sins until he turns away from them.

His saying, "Whoever feared the All-Merciful in the unseen," may be a description of "awwab," or a substitute for "kull" (every), and it may be in the nominative as a subject, the predicate being: "It will be said to them, 'Enter it in peace.'" It may also be a conditional sentence, the response being: "It will be said to them, 'Enter it in peace.'" His saying, "in the unseen," means: without having seen Him; they simply believe in His Messenger and hear His Book. "And came" means: on the Day of Resurrection. "Munib" is one who returns to good and inclines to it. His saying, "Enter it," is an implied "It will be said to them," or "so it will be said to them," as previously stated. "Salam" means: with security and safety from all calamities. His saying, "That is the Day of Eternity," corresponds to His earlier saying concerning the disbelievers: ﴿That is the Day of Threat﴾ [Qaf: 20].

His saying, ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more﴾ is information that they will be given all their hopes in full. Then Allah left vague the increase which He has for the believers who are blessed, and it is likewise vague in His saying: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of the comfort of the eyes﴾ [al-Sajda: 17]. That increase is explained by the sound hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah the Exalted says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, but what I have revealed to them." al-Tabari and others mentioned, in identifying this increase, lengthy narrations and weak matters; for Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿No soul knows﴾ [al-Sajda: 17], and they specify it by forced effort and fervent imagination. It is narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them, that the increase is gazing upon the Face of Allah, the Exalted, without modality.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 50, verses 29–35:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿The Word is not changed with Me, nor am I unjust to the servants.﴾ ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ ﴿And Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing, not far off.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised, for every returner (awwab), keeper (hafiz).﴾ ﴿Whoever feared the All-Merciful in the unseen and came with a contrite heart.﴾ ﴿Enter it in peace; that is the Day of Eternity.﴾ ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more.﴾

The meaning: He has already presented the threat that He will punish the disbelievers in His Fire, so "the Word is not changed with Me," and what My speech has decreed is not diminished. Then He removed the place of objection by His saying, "nor am I unjust to the servants," meaning: this is justice toward them, because I have given warning, granted respite, bestowed faculties of perception, guided them to the path and the two highways, and sent the Messengers. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of His saying, "The Word is not changed with Me," is that it is not falsified before Me, since I have knowledge of all matters; so the reference, according to this, is to the falsehood of the one who said, "I did not make him transgress." His saying, "On the Day We say to Hell," may have as its governing element His saying "nor am I unjust to the servants," and it may be governed by a hidden verb. The majority of reciters, and Hafs from 'Asim, read "naqulu" with the nun, which is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash, and Abu 'Ali preferred it on account of what preceded: His saying "I have sent forward" and His saying "nor am I." Nafi' and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "yaqulu" (He says), meaning Allah says; this is the reading of al-A'raj, Shayba, and the people of Madina. al-Hasan, Ibn Mas'ud, and al-A'mash also read "yuqalu" (it is said) in the passive form.

His saying "Are you filled?" is a questioning for affirmation and confirmation. People differed as to whether this affirmation occurred so that it was filled, or whether it was not filled. Those who held that it was filled, by every opinion of a group of interpreters, interpreted accordingly her saying "Is there any more?" Whoever said that it was filled took her saying, "Is there any more?" to mean a confirmation and negation of more, i.e., "Is there in My presence a place where anything can be added?" A similar interpretation is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And has 'Aqil left us any dwelling?" This is the interpretation of al-Hasan, 'Amr, and Wasil. Whoever said that it was not full took her saying, "Is there any more?" to mean a question and a desire for increase. al-Rummani said: it was said that the meaning is that its guardians say it; but that it is the one speaking is more apparent.

People differed regarding Hell's saying: is it literal or figurative? That is, its state is that of one who, if it spoke, would say such and such; this is like the line:

"My camel complained to me of the length of the journey,"

and like the line of Dhu al-Rummah:

"... its stones and its playgrounds speak to me."

What is preferred regarding Hell's saying, "Is there any more?", is that it is literal, that it said this while not yet full, and this is the saying of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him. A sound, widely transmitted hadith clarifies this, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah says to Hell: Are you filled? It says: Is there any more? until the Mighty One places His foot in it, and it says: Enough, enough, and parts of it draw together with others." People have been at variance regarding the meaning of this hadith. A group of theologians held that "al-Jabbar" (the Mighty One) is a generic noun, and that it refers to the tyrants among the children of Adam. It is narrated that Allah counts among the tyrants a group whom He fills Hell with at the end. It is also narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that the skin of the disbeliever will become forty cubits thick, and his body will grow large in proportion to this; all of this is part of filling Hell. The majority held that al-Jabbar is a name of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and this is the correct view, for in the sound hadith: "So the Lord of the worlds places His foot in it." The interpretation of this is that "qadam" (foot) is what He has sent forward for it from His creation, whom He placed in His knowledge as its inhabitants. From this is His saying: ﴿And give good news to those who believed that they have a sure footing (qadam sidq) with their Lord﴾ [Yunus: 2]. So "qadam" is whatever has been sent forward of a thing. From this is the poet's saying:

"Connect yourself to your Lord and take for yourself a foot (qadam) that will save you on the Day of stumbling and slipping."

From this is al-'Ajjaj's saying:

"... and He establishes kingship for a king of foot (dhi qadam)."

That is, of advanced nobility. This interpretation is narrated from Ibn al-Mubarak and from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, and it is the saying of the scholars of usul. In the book of Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj: "So the Mighty One places His leg in it." Its meaning is the gathering which He has prepared for it; the term "rijl" (leg) is used for a large number of people, by likening them to a locust's leg. The poet said:

"A leg of people passed by it, and there withdrew towards them from the Yemeni tribe a crowd of men."

The criterion for consideration in this hadith is that bodily organ, likeness, and what is similar to them are all negated; nothing remains but the bringing out of expressions in these permissible ways in the speech of the Arabs.

"Uzlifat" means: was brought near. His saying, "not far off," is emphasis and clarification that this nearness is in distance, because "brought near" might have been understood as meaning by promise and information; the possibility was removed by His saying "not far off."

His saying, "This is what you were promised," is the verse. It may mean: it will be said to them in the Hereafter when Paradise is brought near, "This is what you were promised in the world." It may also mean an address to the community of Muhammad ﷺ, i.e., "This is what you, O people, are promised, for every returner (awwab) and keeper (hafiz)." "Awwab" is one who returns to obedience and to the right guidance of his soul. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: the awwab is the one who glorifies (musabbih), from His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10]. al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: he is the one who remembers his sins and seeks forgiveness. al-Muhasibi said: he is the one whose heart turns to Allah, the Exalted. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: we used to say that he is the one who, when he rises from his gathering, seeks Allah's forgiveness for what took place in that gathering, and the Prophet ﷺ used to do likewise. "Hafiz" means: keeping Allah's commands, so that he complies with them, and abandoning His prohibitions. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he is one who guards his sins until he turns away from them.

It may also be a conditional sentence, the response being: "It will be said to them, 'Enter it in peace.'" His saying, "in the unseen," means: without having seen Him; they simply believe in His Messenger and hear His Book. "And came" means: on the Day of Resurrection. "Munib" is one who returns to good and inclines to it. His saying, "Enter it," is an implied "It will be said to them," or "so it will be said to them," as previously stated. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 50, verses 36–40:

The words of the Most High:

﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them, which were stronger than them in might, and they roamed through the lands. Was there any escape?﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness.﴾ ﴿And We certainly created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ ﴿And from the night, glorify Him, and after the prostrations.﴾

"Kam" (how many) is for multiplicity, and it is a declarative (khabariyya) form. The meaning is: "We destroyed many before them." "Al-qarn" (generation) is a community of people over whom a span of time passes. People differed about the length of that span. The majority said it is one hundred years, and other views were stated, which have been discussed more than once before. "Shiddat al-batsh" (great might) refers to abundance of strength, wealth, rule, health, minds, and so on.

The majority of readers read "fa-naqqabu" with a shadda on the qaf, fatha on it, attributing the verb to the past generations. The meaning is: they entered the lands through their passages (anqab). In a hadith: "Upon the passages of Medina are angels, so the plague and the Dajjal will not enter it." The intended meaning is that they wandered and walked about, hoping for deliverance from destruction. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I have searched the horizons until I was content with the gain of returning."

And from it is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza al-Yashkuri:

"They searched the lands, fearing death, and roamed the earth in every direction."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ya'mur, Nassar ibn Yasar, and Abu al-'Aliya read "fa-naqqabu" with a shadda on the qaf, kasra on it, as an imperative addressed to those present. And "hal min mahis" (is there any escape?) is a rhetorical question of rebuke and affirmation, meaning: there is no escape. "Al-mahis" is the place of escape (al-hays), which is swerving and evading. Qatada said: "The disbelievers tried to escape, but they found God's command pursuing them and overtaking them." In the beginning of al-Bukhari there is: "They fled in flight like wild donkeys toward the gates." Ibn 'Abd Shams said describing his she-camel:

"When the guide strays, you see her leaning toward the road in a straight line."

Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Ubayd from him, read "fa-naqabu" with a fatha on the qaf and no shadda. It has the same meaning as the intensive form. The word may also mean searching and seeking. You say: "naqqaba 'an kadhā," meaning he investigated it thoroughly. From this comes "naqib al-qawm" (the leader of the people), because he is the one who searches into their affairs and examines them. In my view, this is a figurative extension of entering through the passages.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder﴾ mean the destruction of those who passed. "Al-dhikra" is a reminder. "Al-qalb" (the heart) is an expression for the intellect, since it is its seat. The meaning is: for whoever has an attentive heart that benefits from it. Al-Shibli said: its meaning is: a heart present with God the Most High that does not neglect Him for the blink of an eye. The words of the Most High ﴿or gives ear while being a witness﴾ mean: he turns his hearing to these admonishing reports and pays attention while listening. That is "ilqa'" (giving) for it, as in His words: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], meaning: I established it upon you. Some people said: the phrase "alqa al-sam'" (gave ear) and His words "So We struck upon their ears" and His words "they were struck with remorse" [al-A'raf: 149] are expressions whose usage has now become rare and whose meanings have become distant. The words of this speaker are weak. Rather, their meanings are clear, and they have been discussed in their places. The words of the Most High "while being a witness" (wa huwa shahid): some interpreters said its meaning is: he is attentive, turned toward the matter, not distracted, and not thinking about anything other than what he hears. Qatada said: it refers to the People of the Book. It is as if He said: indeed, this lesson is a reminder for whoever has understanding, so he reflects upon the matter, or for whoever hears it from the People of the Book, so he bears witness to its truth because he knows it from the Torah and the rest of the books of the Children of Israel. Thus "shahid" on the first interpretation is from witnessing (mushahada), and on the second interpretation is from testimony (shahada). Al-Suddi read "aw alqa al-sam'" (or gave ear), and Ibn Jinni said: meaning "the hearing was cast from him" (uluqiya al-sam' minhu). Abu 'Amr al-Dani relates that the reading of al-Suddi was mentioned to 'Asim, and he disliked al-Suddi and said: "Does not God the Most High say: 'they cast the hearing' (yulqunas-sam')?"

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We certainly created the heavens and the earth﴾ and what follows: this is a report whose content is a refutation of the Jews who said that God created all things in six days and then rested on the Sabbath day. So it was revealed: ﴿and no weariness touched Us.﴾ "Al-lughub" means fatigue, toil, and weariness. It is said: "laghaba al-rajulu yalghubu" when he became tired. Al-Silmi and Talha read "lughub" with a fatha on the lam.

Reports have abundantly stated that the beginning of the creation of things was on Sunday. In Muslim's collection, and in Thabit's Dala'il, there is a hadith whose content is that it was on Saturday. In any case, they agreed that Adam (peace be upon him) was created on Friday. Whoever says the beginning was on Saturday makes the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) like the creation of his children, not counted with the first whole (al-jumla al-ula), and makes the day on which the creatures were completed Friday.

The words of the Most High: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾: some exegetes said the intended people are the People of the Book, because of their saying: "then He rested on the Sabbath day." This statement from the People of the Book was made in Mecca before the Hijra.

The scholarly exegetes (al-nuzzar) said: the words of the Most High ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ are intended to include the People of the Book and other disbelievers. It encompasses all the false sayings of Quraysh and others. On this interpretation, the view of those who say the verse is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword (naskh, abrogation) comes into play. "Sabbih" (glorify) means: pray, by consensus of the interpreters. The words of the Most High "with the praise of your Lord": the "ba'" is for accompaniment (iqtiran), meaning: glorify with a glorification accompanied by praise. Similar is "tanbutu bil-duhn" (it grows with oil) according to some views on it. "Before the rising of the sun" is the dawn prayer, "and before the setting" is the afternoon prayer, as said by Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and the people. Ibn 'Abbas said: "before the setting" is the noon and afternoon prayers. "And from the night" is the prayer of the two evenings (al-'ishā'ayn). Ibn Zayd said: it is the 'Isha' alone. Mujahid said: it is the night prayer. The words of the Most High "and after the prostrations" (wa adbar al-sujud): 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim, Mujahid, and al-Awza'i said: it is the two rak'as after the Maghrib. al-Tabari narrated it with a chain from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ. It seems that the "adbar" of the daytime prayer was considered, just as the "adbar" of the stars is considered in the night prayer. So it was said: it is the two rak'as with the dawn. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that "adbar al-sujud" is the witr prayer, related by al-Tha'labi. Ibn Zayd, and also Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, said: it is the supererogatory prayers after the obligatory prayers, and this accords with the wording of the verse. Some of the knowers of God said: it is the night prayer. Al-Tha'labi said: some scholars said regarding His words "before the rising of the sun" that it is the two rak'as of dawn, and "before the setting" that it is the two rak'as before the Maghrib. One of the Successors said: "I saw the companions of Muhammad ﷺ rushing to them as they rush to the obligatory prayer." Qatada said: "I did not meet anyone who prayed the two rak'as before the Maghrib except Anas and Abu Barza."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Isa, Shibl, Talha, and al-A'mash read "wa idbar" with a kasra on the alif. It is a verbal noun (masdar) to which a time was added, and then the time was omitted, as they say: "ji'tuka maqdim al-hajj" (I came to you at the arrival of the Hajj) and "khafuq al-najm" (at the twinkling of the star) and similar. The rest of the readers, along with al-Hasan and al-A'raj, read "wa adbar" with a fatha on the hamza. It is the plural of "dubur," like "tunub" and "atnab," meaning: and during the latter parts of the prostrations, that is, at their ends. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"After the end of the sacred month, our land and what is around it is barren, the years shining."

The words of the Most High:

﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them, which were stronger than them in might, and they roamed through the lands. Was there any escape?﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while being a witness.﴾ ﴿And We certainly created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.﴾ ﴿And from the night, glorify Him, and after the prostrations.﴾

"Kam" (how many) is for multiplicity, and it is a declarative (khabariyya) form. The meaning is: "We destroyed many before them." "Al-qarn" (generation) is a community of people over whom a span of time passes. People differed about the length of that span. The majority said it is one hundred years, and other views were stated, which have been discussed more than once before. "Shiddat al-batsh" (great might) refers to abundance of strength, wealth, rule, health, minds, and so on.

The majority of readers read "fa-naqqabu" with a shadda on the qaf, fatha on it, attributing the verb to the past generations. The meaning is: they entered the lands through their passages (anqab). In a hadith: "Upon the passages of Medina are angels, so the plague and the Dajjal will not enter it." The intended meaning is that they wandered and walked about, hoping for deliverance from destruction. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I have searched the horizons until I was content with the gain of returning."

And from it is the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza al-Yashkuri:

"They searched the lands, fearing death, and roamed the earth in every direction."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ya'mur, Nassar ibn Yasar, and Abu al-'Aliya read "fa-naqqabu" with a shadda on the qaf, kasra on it, as an imperative addressed to those present. And "hal min mahis" (is there any escape?) is a rhetorical question of rebuke and affirmation, meaning: there is no escape. "Al-mahis" is the place of escape (al-hays), which is swerving and evading. Qatada said: "The disbelievers tried to escape, but they found God's command pursuing them and overtaking them." In the beginning of al-Bukhari there is: "They fled in flight like wild donkeys toward the gates." Ibn 'Abd Shams said describing his she-camel:

"When the guide strays, you see her leaning toward the road in a straight line."

Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Ubayd from him, read "fa-naqabu" with a fatha on the qaf and no shadda. It has the same meaning as the intensive form. The word may also mean searching and seeking. You say: "naqqaba 'an kadhā," meaning he investigated it thoroughly. From this comes "naqib al-qawm" (the leader of the people), because he is the one who searches into their affairs and examines them. In my view, this is a figurative extension of entering through the passages.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder﴾ mean the destruction of those who passed. "Al-dhikra" is a reminder. "Al-qalb" (the heart) is an expression for the intellect, since it is its seat. The meaning is: for whoever has an attentive heart that benefits from it. Al-Shibli said: its meaning is: a heart present with God the Most High that does not neglect Him for the blink of an eye. The words of the Most High ﴿or gives ear while being a witness﴾ mean: he turns his hearing to these admonishing reports and pays attention while listening. That is "ilqa'" (giving) for it, as in His words: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], meaning: I established it upon you. Some people said: the phrase "alqa al-sam'" (gave ear) and His words "So We struck upon their ears" and His words "they were struck with remorse" [al-A'raf: 149] are expressions whose usage has now become rare and whose meanings have become distant. The words of this speaker are weak. Rather, their meanings are clear, and they have been discussed in their places. The words of the Most High "while being a witness" (wa huwa shahid): some interpreters said its meaning is: he is attentive, turned toward the matter, not distracted, and not thinking about anything other than what he hears. Qatada said: it refers to the People of the Book. It is as if He said: indeed, this lesson is a reminder for whoever has understanding, so he reflects upon the matter, or for whoever hears it from the People of the Book, so he bears witness to its truth because he knows it from the Torah and the rest of the books of the Children of Israel. Thus "shahid" on the first interpretation is from witnessing (mushahada), and on the second interpretation is from testimony (shahada). Al-Suddi read "aw alqa al-sam'" (or gave ear), and Ibn Jinni said: meaning "the hearing was cast from him" (uluqiya al-sam' minhu). Abu 'Amr al-Dani relates that the reading of al-Suddi was mentioned to 'Asim, and he disliked al-Suddi and said: "Does not God the Most High say: 'they cast the hearing' (yulqunas-sam')?"

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We certainly created the heavens and the earth﴾ and what follows: this is a report whose content is a refutation of the Jews who said that God created all things in six days and then rested on the Sabbath day. So it was revealed: ﴿and no weariness touched Us.﴾ "Al-lughub" means fatigue, toil, and weariness. It is said: "laghaba al-rajulu yalghubu" when he became tired. Al-Silmi and Talha read "lughub" with a fatha on the lam.

Reports have abundantly stated that the beginning of the creation of things was on Sunday. In Muslim's collection, and in Thabit's Dala'il, there is a hadith whose content is that it was on Saturday. In any case, they agreed that Adam (peace be upon him) was created on Friday. Whoever says the beginning was on Saturday makes the creation of Adam (peace be upon him) like the creation of his children, not counted with the first whole (al-jumla al-ula), and makes the day on which the creatures were completed Friday.

The words of the Most High: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾: some exegetes said the intended people are the People of the Book, because of their saying: "then He rested on the Sabbath day." This statement from the People of the Book was made in Mecca before the Hijra.

The scholarly exegetes (al-nuzzar) said: the words of the Most High ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ are intended to include the People of the Book and other disbelievers. It encompasses all the false sayings of Quraysh and others. On this interpretation, the view of those who say the verse is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword (naskh, abrogation) comes into play. "Sabbih" (glorify) means: pray, by consensus of the interpreters. The words of the Most High "with the praise of your Lord": the "ba'" is for accompaniment (iqtiran), meaning: glorify with a glorification accompanied by praise. Similar is "tanbutu bil-duhn" (it grows with oil) according to some views on it. "Before the rising of the sun" is the dawn prayer, "and before the setting" is the afternoon prayer, as said by Qatada, Ibn Zayd, and the people. Ibn 'Abbas said: "before the setting" is the noon and afternoon prayers. "And from the night" is the prayer of the two evenings (al-'ishā'ayn). Ibn Zayd said: it is the 'Isha' alone. Mujahid said: it is the night prayer. The words of the Most High "and after the prostrations" (wa adbar al-sujud): 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim, Mujahid, and al-Awza'i said: it is the two rak'as after the Maghrib. al-Tabari narrated it with a chain from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ. It seems that the "adbar" of the daytime prayer was considered, just as the "adbar" of the stars is considered in the night prayer. So it was said: it is the two rak'as with the dawn. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that "adbar al-sujud" is the witr prayer, related by al-Tha'labi. Ibn Zayd, and also Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, said: it is the supererogatory prayers after the obligatory prayers, and this accords with the wording of the verse. Some of the knowers of God said: it is the night prayer. Al-Tha'labi said: some scholars said regarding His words "before the rising of the sun" that it is the two rak'as of dawn, and "before the setting" that it is the two rak'as before the Maghrib. One of the Successors said: "I saw the companions of Muhammad ﷺ rushing to them as they rush to the obligatory prayer." Qatada said: "I did not meet anyone who prayed the two rak'as before the Maghrib except Anas and Abu Barza."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Isa, Shibl, Talha, and al-A'mash read "wa idbar" with a kasra on the alif. It is a verbal noun (masdar) to which a time was added, and then the time was omitted, as they say: "ji'tuka maqdim al-hajj" (I came to you at the arrival of the Hajj) and "khafuq al-najm" (at the twinkling of the star) and similar. The rest of the readers, along with al-Hasan and al-A'raj, read "wa adbar" with a fatha on the hamza. It is the plural of "dubur," like "tunub" and "atnab," meaning: and during the latter parts of the prostrations, that is, at their ends. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"After the end of the sacred month, our land and what is around it is barren, the years shining."
